title: Leveling the Playing Field -- Ch. 11: Judicial Excellence in the Bio-Age
keywords: Woodward ex rel. Estate of Woodward v. Commissioner of Social Security
Moore v. Regents of University of California
Commissioner of Patents v. Harvard College
walking encyclopedias of constitutions, laws and judicial doctrines
primary_topics: Chapter 11 of 'Leveling the Playing Field' -- CJP's lecture to a judges' seminar arguing that the bio-age has made legal problems universal, so that judges everywhere must decide the controversies spawned by the biosciences with a common, globalized competence.

His opening argument from the space program -- that the US-USSR space race gave way in the 1990s to the sixteen-nation International Space Station -- as proof that collaboration, not competition, is now the pattern in every field of human endeavor, and that globalization has blurred national legal boundaries and diluted the territoriality doctrine in international law.

A survey of bio-litigation from courts in the United States, Canada and Europe, organized under the Australian Institute of Health, Law and Ethics theme 'Hatching, Matching, Snatching and Dispatching' -- embryo ownership and heirship; GMOs, unapproved drugs and DNA evidence; research and body parts; and the patenting of engineered life.

His closing thesis that deciding the judicial challenges of the third millennium requires overall excellence -- judges who are not merely masters of law but also working students of medicine, economics, computer science, the digital sciences and now the biosciences and biotechnologies.
sub_topics: He opens with a family Christmas in Orlando, Florida -- the Disney Magic Kingdom delighting grandparents and grandchildren alike -- before turning to the visit that really moved him, the Kennedy Space Center at Cape Canaveral.

He recounts the Cold War origins of the space race: Yuri Gagarin orbiting first, President Kennedy's public vow to overtake the USSR, and its fulfillment on July 20, 1969, when Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin walked on the moon.

He notes that the ambition to reach space survived the end of the Cold War, and that the 1990s brought cooperation rather than competition, with Russia and the USA jointly sponsoring the International Space Station, later joined by fourteen more countries for a total of sixteen.

He generalizes the lesson: the shift from bilateral military rivalry to multilateral collaboration typifies globalization in every major human activity, driven by the personal computer, the Internet and the cell phone, with the digitization of information becoming the new means of distributing wealth and power.

He quotes columnist Federico Pascual Jr.'s question-and-answer definition of globalization through the circumstances of Princess Diana's death, then argues that advances in trade, banking, telecommunications, transportation and migration have diluted the territoriality doctrine and are demanding the universalization of laws and of the rulings interpreting them.

He explains why he draws mostly on American bio-cases -- US courts had to grapple early with the new biosciences -- and argues that common problems should be solved similarly by national tribunals to avoid forum shopping and conflicts of jurisdiction.

'Hatching' cases: Kass v. Kass, where the New York Court of Appeals upheld the couple's signed informed consent donating five frozen pre-zygotes to an IVF research program; and J.B. v. M.B., where, absent a controlling contract, the New Jersey court applied public policy to protect the wife's right not to procreate, holding void a contract that would force someone to become a parent later.

Heirship in the bio-age: Woodward ex rel. Estate of Woodward v. Commissioner of Social Security, where the Supreme Judicial Court of Massachusetts balanced three state interests and required proof of the deceased parent's affirmative consent both to posthumous reproduction and to support of the resulting child -- genetic linkage alone being insufficient.

'Matching' cases on access to goods, drugs and treatments: EU labeling rules for GMOs; Monsanto v. Tilly, holding that activists had no right to destroy another's crops absent an emergency; Schiff v. Prados, where a physician was not liable for failing to disclose an illegal antineoplaston treatment unavailable in California; and People v. Privitera, upholding the ban on laetrile as protective of a legitimate state interest.

DNA evidence: he notes that the Supreme Court of his own country has recognized DNA testing as a conclusive means of identifying suspects and establishing filiation, and that abroad DNA has already mutated into post-conviction appeal questions, with Time reporting nearly 80 convicts exonerated by later DNA evidence.

'Snatching' cases on research done on individuals: Moore v. Regents of University of California, where the California Supreme Court grounded a physician's duty to disclose research or economic interests on the patient's right of control, informed consent and the physician's fiduciary duty; and the Maryland lead-paint study, where consent was invalid because parents were not told the children might ingest lead dust.

'Dispatching' cases on ownership of innovations: Diamond v. Chakrabarty, where the US Supreme Court voted 5-4 that an engineered oil-eating bacterium was patentable because the relevant line is between human-made inventions and products of nature; Monsanto v. Schmeiser, upholding the Canola-seed patent; and the oncomouse cases, where US, Japanese and European courts said yes but the Supreme Court of Canada, 5-4, said no in Commissioner of Patents v. Harvard College.
He closes with the demand for overall excellence, presenting the seminar itself as the beginning of judicial competence in the bio-age.

stances.claim: Because the legal problems engendered by the new sciences are themselves universal, the common problems they create should be solved similarly by the various national tribunals, so that forum shopping and conflicts of jurisdiction and judgment are avoided by globalizing justice.
stances.rhetorical_move: analogy from the space program: he moves from bilateral rivalry to sixteen-nation collaboration in space, then transposes that pattern onto adjudication

stances.claim: Globalization has blurred national legal boundaries and diluted the territoriality doctrine, so that a new paradigm is emerging which demands the universalization of laws and of the judicial rulings interpreting them.
stances.rhetorical_move: accumulation of evidence -- trade, banking, telecommunications, transportation, migration and the Princess Diana anecdote stacked to make the erosion of borders feel self-evident

stances.claim: It is no longer enough for judges to be walking encyclopedias of constitutions, laws and judicial doctrines; they must also have a working knowledge of most branches of human knowledge, including the biosciences and biotechnologies.
stances.rhetorical_move: cumulative case-survey then demand: eleven foreign bio-cases are marched past the audience so the concluding call for overall excellence reads as the only possible inference

stances.claim: The bio-cases he surveys were, in the main, correctly resolved on the courts' own terms -- dispositional intent controlling where clear, public policy where it is not, and informed consent and fiduciary disclosure governing research on patients.
stances.rhetorical_move: neutral case reportage: he restates each holding and its reasoning without dissenting, letting the doctrines stand as instruction rather than argument

notable_anecdotes: Christmas in Orlando: he recalls spending the holidays two months earlier with his wife, children, their spouses and his grandchildren, all of them impressed by Mickey Mouse and Donald Duck at the Disney Magic Kingdom.
The Kennedy Space Center tour: what specially delighted him was the nearby visit to Cape Canaveral, where the guided account of the 1960s space race framed the whole lecture.

Kennedy's vow: he retells how, to President Kennedy's chagrin, the Russian Yuri Gagarin orbited first, prompting the public promise that America would put the first humans on the moon -- kept on July 20, 1969.

The Princess Diana definition of globalization: he quotes columnist Federico Pascual Jr.'s question-and-answer joke about an English princess, an Egyptian boyfriend, a French tunnel, a German car and a drunk Belgian driver as the truest definition of globalization.
Cloning a lawyer: he reports with amusement that at the AIHLE conference the medicolegal debate asked whether it would be ethical to clone a lawyer.

The spleen case: he recounts how Moore's doctor extracted blood, serum, skin, bone marrow and sperm and then recommended removing his spleen, using the organ to establish a cell line for his own research.
Eighty exonerations: he cites a Time magazine report that in the United States alone nearly 80 convicts under final judgments were later cleared when DNA evidence proved them innocent.

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 11 of 'Leveling the Playing Field' is CJP's lecture on judicial excellence in the bio-age, opening with a family Christmas in Orlando and, more consequentially for him, a tour of the Kennedy Space Center at Cape Canaveral. He retold how the Cold War drove the space race -- Yuri Gagarin orbiting first, Kennedy vowing America would reach the moon, Armstrong and Aldrin fulfilling that vow on July 20, 1969 -- and then observed that the 1990s replaced competition with cooperation, as Russia and the United States jointly built the International Space Station and fourteen other nations joined them. That shift, he argued, typifies globalization in every field: the personal computer, the Internet and the cell phone have made the world one global village in which traditional legal borders no longer deter human progress, and advances in trade, banking, telecommunications, transportation and migration have diluted the territoriality doctrine, so that a new paradigm demands the universalization of laws and of the rulings interpreting them. Quoting columnist Federico Pascual Jr.'s joke defining globalization through Princess Diana's death, he moved to his substance: a survey of bio-litigation organized under the Australian Institute of Health, Law and Ethics theme 'Hatching, Matching, Snatching and Dispatching.' Under hatching he discussed Kass v. Kass and J.B. v. M.B. on the disposition of frozen pre-embryos and Woodward on the inheritance rights of posthumously conceived children; under matching, EU labeling of GMOs, Monsanto v. Tilly, Schiff v. Prados, People v. Privitera and the rise of DNA evidence, including Time's report of nearly eighty DNA exonerations; under snatching, Moore v. Regents of University of California, the Maryland lead-paint study and Pate v. Threlkel on disclosure, consent and fiduciary duty; and under dispatching, Diamond v. Chakrabarty, Monsanto v. Schmeiser and the divided oncomouse rulings on patenting engineered life. Because such disputes will occur worldwide, he urged that national tribunals resolve them similarly, avoiding forum shopping by globalizing justice, and concluded that it is no longer enough for judges to be walking encyclopedias of law -- they must command the humanities, economics, medicine, the digital sciences and now the biosciences as well.
